claim: Hippocampal replay is the time-compressed, sequential reactivation of ensembles of neurons related to past experience.
source: Hippocampal replay – the time-compressed, sequential reactivation of ensembles of neurons related to past experience – is a key neural mechanism of memory consolidation.
evidence: This is a definitional statement that draws from established scientific understanding of hippocampal replay.

claim: Hippocampal replay is a key neural mechanism of memory consolidation.
source: Hippocampal replay – the time-compressed, sequential reactivation of ensembles of neurons related to past experience – is a key neural mechanism of memory consolidation.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific consensus about the role of replay in memory.

claim: Replay typically coincides with sharp-wave ripples (SWRs).
source: Replay typically coincides with a characteristic pattern of local field potential activity, the sharp-wave ripple (SWR).
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about the relationship between replay and SWRs.

claim: Reduced SWR rates are associated with cognitive impairment in multiple models of neurodegenerative disease.
source: Reduced SWR rates are associated with cognitive impairment in multiple models of neurodegenerative disease, suggesting that a clinically viable intervention to promote SWRs and replay would prove beneficial.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on SWRs in disease models mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: The neurofeedback training protocol increased the prevalence of task-relevant replay during the targeted neurofeedback period.
source: This training protocol increased the prevalence of task-relevant replay during the targeted neurofeedback period by changing the temporal dynamics of SWR occurrence.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The neurofeedback training protocol changed the temporal dynamics of SWR occurrence.
source: This training protocol increased the prevalence of task-relevant replay during the targeted neurofeedback period by changing the temporal dynamics of SWR occurrence.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing changes in when SWRs occurred.

claim: The increase in replay was associated with neural and behavioral forms of compensation after the targeted period.
source: This increase was also associated with neural and behavioral forms of compensation after the targeted period.
evidence: This is supported by data showing changes in post-reward SWR patterns and dwell times.

claim: Neurofeedback is an effective strategy for modulating hippocampal replay.
source: These findings reveal short-timescale regulation of SWR generation and demonstrate that neurofeedback is an effective strategy for modulating hippocampal replay.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: SWR generation is regulated on short timescales.
source: These findings reveal short-timescale regulation of SWR generation and demonstrate that neurofeedback is an effective strategy for modulating hippocampal replay.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed compensatory changes in SWR patterns within trials.

claim: Patterns of neural activity associated with past experience are replayed during offline states such as sleep and pauses in ongoing behavior.
source: Subsequently, patterns of neural activity associated with past experience are 'replayed' during offline states, such as sleep and pauses in ongoing behavior (Findlay et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Replay events tend to coincide with sharp wave ripples (SWRs).
source: Replay events tend to coincide with sharp wave ripples (SWRs), characteristic bursts of high-frequency oscillatory activity in the CA1 region of the hippocampus that coordinate spiking activity in a wide range of cortical and subcortical brain regions (Buzsáki, 2015; Joo and Frank, 2018; Skelin et al., 2019; Todorova and Zugaro, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: SWRs are characteristic bursts of high-frequency oscillatory activity in the CA1 region of the hippocampus.
source: Replay events tend to coincide with sharp wave ripples (SWRs), characteristic bursts of high-frequency oscillatory activity in the CA1 region of the hippocampus that coordinate spiking activity in a wide range of cortical and subcortical brain regions (Buzsáki, 2015; Joo and Frank, 2018; Skelin et al., 2019; Todorova and Zugaro, 2020).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations.

claim: SWRs coordinate spiking activity in a wide range of cortical and subcortical brain regions.
source: Replay events tend to coincide with sharp wave ripples (SWRs), characteristic bursts of high-frequency oscillatory activity in the CA1 region of the hippocampus that coordinate spiking activity in a wide range of cortical and subcortical brain regions (Buzsáki, 2015; Joo and Frank, 2018; Skelin et al., 2019; Todorova and Zugaro, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Brain-wide coordination of activity during SWRs enables their proposed role in storing and maintaining memory traces in distributed hippocampal-cortical circuits.
source: The brain-wide coordination of activity during SWRs is thought to enable their proposed role in storing and maintaining memory traces in distributed hippocampal-cortical circuits (Frankland and Bontempi, 2005; Kaefer et al., 2022; Klinzing et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Disrupting SWRs impairs learning and alters memory performance.
source: Disrupting SWRs impairs learning and alters memory performance, establishing the necessity of SWRs for intact memory-guided behavior (Aleman-Zapata et al., 2022; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010; Girardeau et al., 2009; Jadhav et al., 2012; Nokia et al., 2012; Todorova and Zugaro, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: SWRs are necessary for intact memory-guided behavior.
source: Disrupting SWRs impairs learning and alters memory performance, establishing the necessity of SWRs for intact memory-guided behavior (Aleman-Zapata et al., 2022; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010; Girardeau et al., 2009; Jadhav et al., 2012; Nokia et al., 2012; Todorova and Zugaro, 2020).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from cited studies showing impairments when SWRs are disrupted.

claim: Reductions and abnormalities in SWRs occur concurrent with memory impairment in several rodent models of neurological disease.
source: The importance of SWRs to memory function is further underscored by observations of reductions and abnormalities in SWRs concurrent with memory impairment in several rodent models of neurological disease (Gillespie et al., 2016; Iaccarino et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2019; Prince et al., 2021; Sanchez-Aguilera and Quintanilla, 2021; Stoiljkovic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research in disease models.

claim: Driving or enhancing SWRs in cases where they are compromised could confer therapeutic benefit.
source: These findings raise the compelling possibility that driving or enhancing SWRs in cases where they are compromised could confer therapeutic benefit.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from prior findings about SWR deficits in disease.

claim: Electrical stimulation and optogenetics have been used to evoke exogenous SWRs.
source: Electrical stimulation and optogenetics have been used to evoke exogenous SWRs (Ishikawa et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2018; Stark et al., 2015; Stark et al., 2014, Oliva et al., 2020) or to enhance existing SWRs (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Maingret et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Electrical stimulation and optogenetics have been used to enhance existing SWRs.
source: Electrical stimulation and optogenetics have been used to evoke exogenous SWRs (Ishikawa et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2018; Stark et al., 2015; Stark et al., 2014, Oliva et al., 2020) or to enhance existing SWRs (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Maingret et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Some studies have demonstrated the selective engagement of subsets of hippocampal neurons during SWR manipulations.
source: In some cases, studies have demonstrated the selective engagement of subsets of hippocampal neurons (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Oliva et al., 2020), but whether these manipulations preserve the full diversity or accuracy of naturally occurring replay events remains unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific prior studies.

claim: Whether SWR manipulations preserve the full diversity or accuracy of naturally occurring replay events remains unknown.
source: In some cases, studies have demonstrated the selective engagement of subsets of hippocampal neurons (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Oliva et al., 2020), but whether these manipulations preserve the full diversity or accuracy of naturally occurring replay events remains unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge based on limitations of prior studies.

claim: Endogenous SWRs tend to occur within permissive windows influenced by cortical activity states.
source: Further, endogenous SWRs tend to occur within permissive windows influenced by cortical activity states (Battaglia et al., 2004; Isomura et al., 2006) and neuromodulatory tone (Novitskaya et al., 2016; Vandecasteele et al., 2014); it is unclear whether exogenous events evoked outside of such states recruit downstream targets or engage brain-wide coordination as endogenous SWRs do.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Endogenous SWRs tend to occur within permissive windows influenced by neuromodulatory tone.
source: Further, endogenous SWRs tend to occur within permissive windows influenced by cortical activity states (Battaglia et al., 2004; Isomura et al., 2006) and neuromodulatory tone (Novitskaya et al., 2016; Vandecasteele et al., 2014); it is unclear whether exogenous events evoked outside of such states recruit downstream targets or engage brain-wide coordination as endogenous SWRs do.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is unclear whether exogenous SWR events evoked outside of permissive states recruit downstream targets or engage brain-wide coordination as endogenous SWRs do.
source: Further, endogenous SWRs tend to occur within permissive windows influenced by cortical activity states (Battaglia et al., 2004; Isomura et al., 2006) and neuromodulatory tone (Novitskaya et al., 2016; Vandecasteele et al., 2014); it is unclear whether exogenous events evoked outside of such states recruit downstream targets or engage brain-wide coordination as endogenous SWRs do.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge about artificially evoked SWRs.

claim: Both electrical and optogenetic interventions are suboptimal for translation to human use.
source: Finally, both electrical and optogenetic interventions are suboptimal for translation to human use.
evidence: This is an inference based on the practical limitations of these techniques.

claim: Both electrical and optogenetic interventions would require invasive procedures.
source: Both approaches would require invasive procedures, and clinical use of optogenetics in the brain faces even more fundamental barriers (White et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of how these techniques are implemented.

claim: Clinical use of optogenetics in the brain faces fundamental barriers.
source: Both approaches would require invasive procedures, and clinical use of optogenetics in the brain faces even more fundamental barriers (White et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work discussing these barriers.

claim: Neurofeedback enables subjects to alter their own brain states through real-time external feedback.
source: Neurofeedback, wherein subjects are given real-time external feedback that allows them to alter their own brain states, has been shown to enable modulation of patterns of brain activity across species (Sitaram et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by a citation.

claim: Neurofeedback has been shown to enable modulation of patterns of brain activity across species.
source: Neurofeedback, wherein subjects are given real-time external feedback that allows them to alter their own brain states, has been shown to enable modulation of patterns of brain activity across species (Sitaram et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The efficacy of neurofeedback-based therapy has been established for ADHD and stroke.
source: The efficacy of neurofeedback-based therapy has been established for some clinical indications, such as ADHD and stroke, but the use of neurofeedback for memory-related symptoms has shown variable efficacy (Staufenbiel et al., 2014; Wang and Hsieh, 2013) and is still in early stages (Jiang et al., 2022; Klink et al., 2021; Trambaiolli et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical research.

claim: The use of neurofeedback for memory-related symptoms has shown variable efficacy.
source: The efficacy of neurofeedback-based therapy has been established for some clinical indications, such as ADHD and stroke, but the use of neurofeedback for memory-related symptoms has shown variable efficacy (Staufenbiel et al., 2014; Wang and Hsieh, 2013) and is still in early stages (Jiang et al., 2022; Klink et al., 2021; Trambaiolli et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The use of neurofeedback for memory-related symptoms is still in early stages.
source: The efficacy of neurofeedback-based therapy has been established for some clinical indications, such as ADHD and stroke, but the use of neurofeedback for memory-related symptoms has shown variable efficacy (Staufenbiel et al., 2014; Wang and Hsieh, 2013) and is still in early stages (Jiang et al., 2022; Klink et al., 2021; Trambaiolli et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Most neurofeedback paradigms target the modulation of oscillatory activity in specific frequency bands linked to cognitive functions.
source: Moreover, most neurofeedback paradigms target the modulation of oscillatory activity in specific frequency bands linked to cognitive functions, such as gamma or theta (Engelhard et al., 2013; Reiner et al., 2014; Wang and Hsieh, 2013) or overall activity levels (Klink et al., 2021), rather than focusing on specific memory-related hippocampal activity patterns (e.g. SWRs).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior neurofeedback studies.

claim: Prior work using intracranial stimulation of a reward-related brain region achieved operant conditioning of SWRs.
source: We therefore asked whether providing external positive neurofeedback coupled to SWRs would effectively drive SWR occurrence, a possibility consistent with prior work using intracranial stimulation of a reward-related brain region to achieve operant conditioning of SWRs (Ishikawa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific prior study.

claim: Replay during SWRs is thought to be central to their function.
source: Further, since the replay during SWRs is thought to be central to their function, we also sought to evaluate whether SWR-based neurofeedback could drive replay events with physiologically relevant spatial content.
evidence: This reflects established scientific understanding about the importance of replay.

claim: The neurofeedback training paradigm increases the rates of SWRs during the targeted neurofeedback period.
source: We were able to develop a neurofeedback training paradigm for rats that increases the rates of SWRs and replay during the targeted neurofeedback period.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The neurofeedback training paradigm increases the rates of replay during the targeted neurofeedback period.
source: We were able to develop a neurofeedback training paradigm for rats that increases the rates of SWRs and replay during the targeted neurofeedback period.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: SWRs during the targeted period were reliably associated with replay events which represented a range of spatial content consistent with that seen in a previous study.
source: Importantly, SWRs during the targeted period were reliably associated with replay events which represented a range of spatial content consistent with that seen in our previous study of replay in a very similar task (Gillespie et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and comparison to prior work.

claim: Compensatory changes were observed outside of the targeted neurofeedback period.
source: Interestingly, we also observed some compensatory changes outside of the targeted neurofeedback period.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing changes in post-reward periods.

claim: SWR generation during task performance is influenced by homeostatic regulation on the timescale of seconds.
source: Further, they suggest that SWR generation during task performance is influenced by homeostatic regulation on the timescale of seconds, an important factor to consider when developing strategies to drive SWRs and replay therapeutically.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed compensatory changes in SWR patterns.

claim: In the neurofeedback paradigm, SWR detection triggered rapid positive feedback in the context of a memory-dependent task.
source: To reinforce SWR activity, our neurofeedback paradigm linked the online detection of large SWRs with positive reinforcement: delivery of a tone and food reward (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design implemented in the study.

claim: The neurofeedback paradigm was embedded into a flexible spatial memory task.
source: We embedded the neurofeedback requirement into a flexible spatial memory task (Figure 1B) that we have studied extensively (Gillespie et al., 2021), allowing us to compare neural and behavioral data from subjects that perform the task with neurofeedback manipulation to those without the manipulation component.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Subjects in the manipulation cohort successfully produced increasingly large trigger events at the neurofeedback port over the course of training.
source: In response to the increasing SWR detection threshold, subjects in the manipulation cohort successfully produced increasingly large trigger events at the neurofeedback port over the course of training (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increasing trigger event sizes.

claim: Subjects learned a strategy for generating large events that allowed them to meet the neurofeedback criteria more efficiently.
source: This suggests that subjects learned a strategy for generating large events that allowed them to meet the neurofeedback criteria more efficiently.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that wait times were shorter than predicted.

claim: Subjects did not consistently increase SWR size in response to neurofeedback training.
source: First, to assess whether subjects learned to directly increase the size of SWR events, we quantified the mean size of SWRs that occured pre-reward at the center ports on neurofeedback and delay trials during behavioral epochs from the stable period. Importantly, to account for the structure of the task, we excluded suprathreshold events detected by our online algorithm during both neurofeedback and delay trials (see Methods). These analyses revealed that subjects did not consistently increase SWR size: only two out of four subjects showed very slight but significant increases (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of SWR sizes across trial types.

claim: There was no difference in SWR size between either trial type in the manipulation cohort and the control cohort.
source: We also found no difference in SWR size between either trial type in the manipulation cohort and the control cohort (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, inset).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison between cohorts.

claim: Within the manipulation cohort, neurofeedback trials contained roughly twice as many events relative to delay trials for all SWR sizes.
source: Instead, when we quantified the number of events of each size per behavioral epoch, we found that within the manipulation cohort, neurofeedback trials contained roughly twice as many events relative to delay trials for all SWR sizes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of SWR counts by size.

claim: Subjects met the neurofeedback criteria efficiently by modulating SWR rate, not event size.
source: These results rule out our first candidate strategy and indicate that subjects met the neurofeedback criteria efficiently by modulating SWR rate, not event size.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the data showing increased SWR counts but not sizes.

claim: Subjects in the manipulation cohort showed high, stable SWR rates before reward delivery, with neurofeedback trials showing higher SWR rate than delay trials.
source: Subjects in the manipulation cohort all showed high, stable SWR rates before reward delivery, with neurofeedback trials showing higher SWR rate than delay trials.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of SWR rates in time bins aligned to reward delivery.

claim: Subjects in the control cohort rarely generated SWRs during the pre-reward period but showed much higher SWR rates than the manipulation cohort after reward delivery.
source: By contrast, subjects in the control cohort rarely generated SWRs during the pre-reward period but showed much higher SWR rates than the manipulation cohort after reward delivery.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of SWR rates across time periods and cohorts.

claim: During the pre-reward period, SWR rates were approximately twice as high on neurofeedback compared to delay trials.
source: Indeed, we found that during the pre-reward period, SWR rates were approximately twice as high on neurofeedback compared to delay trials, and both trial types from the manipulation cohort had much higher rates than trials from the control cohort (Figure 2C, left).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of SWR rates.

claim: Both neurofeedback and delay trial types from the manipulation cohort had much higher SWR rates than trials from the control cohort during the pre-reward period.
source: Indeed, we found that during the pre-reward period, SWR rates were approximately twice as high on neurofeedback compared to delay trials, and both trial types from the manipulation cohort had much higher rates than trials from the control cohort (Figure 2C, left).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis comparing cohorts.

claim: The neurofeedback training caused far more SWRs to occur prior to reward delivery at both center ports in the manipulation cohort.
source: This finding indicates that the neurofeedback training caused far more SWRs to occur prior to reward delivery at both center ports in the manipulation cohort, with the most pronounced effect occurring on neurofeedback trials.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the SWR rate data.

claim: SWR rate was slightly but significantly higher during delay trials compared to neurofeedback trials in the manipulation cohort subjects during the post-reward period.
source: These patterns differed after the reward at the center ports, where SWR rate was slightly but significantly higher during delay trials compared to neurofeedback trials in the manipulation cohort subjects but was overall indistinguishable between the cohorts (Figure 2C, middle).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of post-reward SWR rates.

claim: Post-reward SWR rate was overall indistinguishable between the cohorts.
source: These patterns differed after the reward at the center ports, where SWR rate was slightly but significantly higher during delay trials compared to neurofeedback trials in the manipulation cohort subjects but was overall indistinguishable between the cohorts (Figure 2C, middle).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison between cohorts.

claim: When considering both pre- and post-reward periods together, the neurofeedback trials showed higher SWR rates than delay trials within the manipulation cohort.
source: When considering both pre- and post-reward periods together, the neurofeedback trials still showed higher SWR rates than delay trials within the manipulation cohort, but the differences between each trial type and the control cohort were not significant (Figure 2C, right).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of combined period SWR rates.

claim: The differences in total SWR rate between each trial type and the control cohort were not significant.
source: When considering both pre- and post-reward periods together, the neurofeedback trials still showed higher SWR rates than delay trials within the manipulation cohort, but the differences between each trial type and the control cohort were not significant (Figure 2C, right).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The pre-reward effects on SWR rate in the manipulation cohort were followed by compensatory effects post-reward that resulted in a net normalization of total SWR rate across cohorts.
source: This surprising result suggested that the pre-reward effects on SWR rate in the manipulation cohort were followed by some compensatory effects post-reward that resulted in a net normalization of total SWR rate across cohorts.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of SWR rates across time periods.

claim: During the post-reward period, neurofeedback trials contained fewer SWRs than delay trials.
source: However, we found striking differences during the post-reward period, during which we saw a clear reversal of the pre-reward effect on SWR counts: neurofeedback trials contained fewer SWRs than delay trials, and both trial types contained far fewer SWRs post-reward than trials from the control cohort (Figure 2D, center).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of SWR counts.

claim: Both neurofeedback and delay trial types contained far fewer SWRs post-reward than trials from the control cohort.
source: However, we found striking differences during the post-reward period, during which we saw a clear reversal of the pre-reward effect on SWR counts: neurofeedback trials contained fewer SWRs than delay trials, and both trial types contained far fewer SWRs post-reward than trials from the control cohort (Figure 2D, center).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis comparing cohorts.

claim: The compensatory effect involves the amount of time spent at the port post-reward.
source: Since post-reward SWR rates were not different between the cohorts, the count results indicated that the compensatory effect must involve the amount of time spent at the port post-reward.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of rate and count data.

claim: Neurofeedback trials had slightly but significantly shorter post-reward periods than delay trials.
source: Indeed, we found clear differences in the amount of time that subjects chose to spend at the port after reward delivery. Here it is important to remember that in contrast to the pre-reward dwell time, which is imposed by task constraints, the post-reward dwell time is not externally constrained. It was notable, therefore, that neurofeedback trials had slightly but significantly shorter post-reward periods than delay trials (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of dwell times.

claim: Subjects in the manipulation cohort remained at the port for approximately half as long as subjects in the control cohort after reward delivery.
source: Even more strikingly, subjects in the manipulation cohort remained at the port for approximately half as long as subjects in the control cohort (Figure 2E, inset), despite all trial types receiving the same amount of reward.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative comparison of post-reward dwell times.

claim: Both covert and overt processes regulate SWR generation.
source: Together, these findings suggest that both covert and overt processes regulate SWR generation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of SWR rate changes and behavioral changes.

claim: Animals learned to modulate their SWR rate when required during the pre-reward period of neurofeedback trials covertly, without displaying obvious behavioral correlates.
source: Animals learned to modulate their SWR rate when required during the pre-reward period of neurofeedback trials and did so covertly, without displaying obvious behavioral correlates.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased SWR rates without major behavioral changes during the pre-reward period.

claim: An overt change in behavior (leaving the well early) was associated with lower numbers of SWRs post-reward in the neurofeedback cohort.
source: A subsequent overt change in behavior – leaving the well early – was then associated with lower numbers of SWRs post-reward in the neurofeedback cohort.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between shorter dwell times and fewer SWRs post-reward.

claim: The mean speeds of the head-mounted LEDs while the subjects were nosepoked were below the cutoff for immobility (4 cm/s) for all trial types.
source: The mean speeds of the head-mounted LEDs while the subjects were nosepoked were below our cutoff for immobility (4 cm/s) for all trial types, however, we did observe a slightly but significantly lower mean speed during the pre-reward period on neurofeedback trials compared to delay trials and trials from the control cohort (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of movement speeds.

claim: A slightly but significantly lower mean speed was observed during the pre-reward period on neurofeedback trials compared to delay trials and trials from the control cohort.
source: The mean speeds of the head-mounted LEDs while the subjects were nosepoked were below our cutoff for immobility (4 cm/s) for all trial types, however, we did observe a slightly but significantly lower mean speed during the pre-reward period on neurofeedback trials compared to delay trials and trials from the control cohort (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of movement speeds.

claim: Even with much higher mean speeds, neurofeedback trials showed higher SWR rates than control and delay trials.
source: Even with much higher mean speeds (Figure 3B), the neurofeedback trials showed higher SWR rates than control and delay trials (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of SWR rates in speed-matched trial subsets.

claim: Movement differences during the time spent at the center ports cannot explain the increased SWR rates observed prior to reward during neurofeedback trials.
source: This analysis suggests that movement differences during the time spent at the center ports cannot explain the increased SWR rates observed prior to reward during neurofeedback trials.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the speed-matched analysis showing persistent SWR rate differences.

claim: The stability of total SWR rate and count at both center ports across the two cohorts suggests that some regulatory mechanisms keep SWR generation within a set range for the center port phase of this task.
source: The surprising stability of total SWR rate and count at both center ports across the two cohorts, despite changes in when those SWRs occurred relative to reward delivery, suggests that some regulatory mechanisms keep SWR generation within a set range for the center port phase of this task.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of compensatory changes that normalize total SWR counts.

claim: There was no consistent evidence for strict regulation of SWR generation within a single trial.
source: However, we did not find evidence for such a relationship consistently: the correlation coefficients between pre-reward and post-reward SWR counts were positive in some subjects and negative in others, and always very small in magnitude, indicating a weak relationship (r=–0.084, 0.130. 0.118, and –0.061 and p=1.47 × 10–7, 3.84x10–6, 8.60x10–9, and 6.01x10–4, for each subject in the manipulation cohort, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of pre- and post-reward SWR counts.

claim: While compensatory regulation of SWR generation may be evident across hundreds of trials, high variability in SWR rate, count, and dwell time across trials may prevent consistent detection of this effect at the level of single trials.
source: These results suggest that while compensatory regulation of SWR generation may be evident across hundreds of trials, high variability in SWR rate, count, and dwell time across trials may prevent consistent detection of this effect at the level of single trials.
evidence: This is inferred from the weak trial-by-trial correlations despite clear group-level effects.

claim: Hippocampal CA1 neurons often fire reliably at particular locations in space ('place cells') while an animal moves through an environment.
source: As hippocampal CA1 neurons often fire reliably at particular locations in space ('place cells') while an animal moves through an environment, replay content has most often been studied with regard to its spatial content.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about place cells.

claim: A clusterless state-space model was used to decode spatial content of replay.
source: We used a clusterless state-space model (Chen et al., 2012; Deng et al., 2016; Denovellis et al., 2021; Kloosterman et al., 2014) identical to the one we used previously to characterize the spatial content of replay for the animals in the control cohort (Gillespie et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the analytical method used, supported by citations.

claim: There was no difference in the fraction of SWRs that qualified as replay between the two cohorts during the pre-reward period.
source: In SWRs during the pre-reward period, there was no difference in the fraction of SWRs that qualified as replay between the two cohorts, and within each manipulation cohort subject, there was no consistent difference between neurofeedback and delay trials (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of replay fractions.

claim: Within each manipulation cohort subject, there was no consistent difference in the fraction of SWRs that qualified as replay between neurofeedback and delay trials during the pre-reward period.
source: In SWRs during the pre-reward period, there was no difference in the fraction of SWRs that qualified as replay between the two cohorts, and within each manipulation cohort subject, there was no consistent difference between neurofeedback and delay trials (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Replay of remote locations has been proposed to play a particularly important role in updating or maintaining memory in the absence of direct experience.
source: Replay of remote locations has been proposed to play a particularly important role in updating or maintaining memory in the absence of direct experience (Gillespie et al., 2021; Gupta et al., 2010; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There were much higher rates of remote replay during the pre-reward period in neurofeedback trials compared to delay trials within the manipulation cohort.
source: Consistent with our SWR findings, we find much higher rates of remote replay during the pre-reward period in neurofeedback trials compared to delay trials within the manipulation cohort, and low rates of remote replay during this time in trials from the control cohort (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of remote replay rates.

claim: There were low rates of remote replay during the pre-reward period in trials from the control cohort.
source: Consistent with our SWR findings, we find much higher rates of remote replay during the pre-reward period in neurofeedback trials compared to delay trials within the manipulation cohort, and low rates of remote replay during this time in trials from the control cohort (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis.

claim: There was no difference in remote replay rate between the two cohorts when considering both the pre- and post-reward periods combined.
source: However, if we consider both the pre-and post-reward periods combined, we find no difference in remote replay rate between the two cohorts for either trial type (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of combined period replay rates.

claim: Within the manipulation cohort, neurofeedback trials have slightly but significantly higher rates of remote replay than delay trials over the combined pre- and post-reward period.
source: Within the manipulation cohort, neurofeedback trials have slightly but significantly higher rates of remote replay than delay trials over the combined pre- and post-reward period.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Replay events in this task were enriched for specific, relevant past experiences that change as a function of goal location.
source: Prior work demonstrated that replay events in this task were enriched for specific, relevant past experiences that change as a function of goal location (Gillespie et al., 2021), and we saw the same biases in replay content in the manipulation cohort.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and confirmed by current data.

claim: Enhanced representation of previous goal locations was observed in replay events during the pre-reward period in both neurofeedback and delay trials within the manipulation cohort.
source: As previously seen in the control cohort, we observed consistently enhanced representation of previous goal locations in replay events during the pre-reward period in both neurofeedback and delay trials within the manipulation cohort (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by GLM analysis of replay content.

claim: Reduced prevalence of replay representing the immediately previously visited arm was observed.
source: Similarly, we replicated the reduced prevalence of replay representing the immediately previously visited arm and a slightly increased prevalence of replay of the arm associated with the upcoming choice in both trial types of the manipulation cohort.
evidence: This is supported by GLM analysis of replay content.

claim: A slightly increased prevalence of replay of the arm associated with the upcoming choice was observed in both trial types of the manipulation cohort.
source: Similarly, we replicated the reduced prevalence of replay representing the immediately previously visited arm and a slightly increased prevalence of replay of the arm associated with the upcoming choice in both trial types of the manipulation cohort.
evidence: This is supported by GLM analysis.

claim: While the timing of replay is altered by the neurofeedback training, the content and behavioral relevance is preserved.
source: Together, these results indicate that while the timing of replay is altered by the neurofeedback training, the content and behavioral relevance is preserved.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the replay content analysis showing preserved spatial biases.

claim: SWRs and remote replay rate were generally indistinguishable between the manipulation and control cohorts when the total time at the center ports was considered.
source: Since SWRs and remote replay rate were generally indistinguishable between the manipulation and control cohorts when the total time at the center ports was considered, we did not expect to find a large difference in behavior between the two cohorts.
evidence: This is based on the data showing normalized total SWR and replay rates.

claim: The manipulation cohort subjects show a slight improvement in search efficiency compared to control subjects, which only reached significance on delay trials.
source: The manipulation cohort subjects show a slight improvement in search efficiency compared to control subjects, which only reached significance on delay trials (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of search efficiency.

claim: The difference in search efficiency could have been driven by the additional days of experience that the manipulation cohort has on the task.
source: However, rather than relating to the neurofeedback training, this difference could have been driven by the additional days of experience that the manipulation cohort has on the task, since the control cohort showed a subtle but consistent increase in this performance measure over time (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that search efficiency increases with experience in the control cohort.

claim: There was no significant difference in search efficiency between neurofeedback and delay trials.
source: Consistent with this possibility, we find no significant difference in this metric between neurofeedback and delay trials.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Neurofeedback trials accounted for approximately half of redundant search trials for each subject.
source: We found no bias toward either of the two trial types: neurofeedback trials accounted for approximately half of redundant search trials for each subject (Figure 5B), indicating that neither the neurofeedback nor delay trial type was consistently overrepresented among the trials with suboptimal behavior.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of trial type distribution.

claim: Neither the neurofeedback nor delay trial type was consistently overrepresented among the trials with suboptimal behavior.
source: We found no bias toward either of the two trial types: neurofeedback trials accounted for approximately half of redundant search trials for each subject (Figure 5B), indicating that neither the neurofeedback nor delay trial type was consistently overrepresented among the trials with suboptimal behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the equal distribution of trial types among errors.

claim: There was no difference between the two cohorts or between neurofeedback and delay trials in the fraction of trials during which the subject correctly visited the goal arm.
source: To quantify performance during trials when the goal arm had already been discovered by the subject and should be chosen again ('repeat' trials), we measured the fraction of subsequent trials during which the subject correctly visited the goal arm. We also saw no difference between the two cohorts or between neurofeedback and delay trials on this measure (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of repeat trial performance.

claim: Error trials were equally distributed between neurofeedback and delay trials within the manipulation cohort.
source: Within the manipulation cohort, we also found that error trials, when subjects do not choose to visit a known goal arm, were equally distributed between neurofeedback and delay trials (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of error trial distribution.

claim: On a single-trial timescale, the neurofeedback manipulation had neither a beneficial nor detrimental effect on behavior.
source: Overall, these results suggest that on a single-trial timescale, the neurofeedback manipulation had neither a beneficial nor detrimental effect on behavior, in line with our previous findings (Gillespie et al., 2021).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the behavioral performance data and is consistent with prior work.

claim: The study substantially extends a prior demonstration of operant conditioning of SWRs in three important ways.
source: These results substantially extend a prior demonstration of operant conditioning of SWRs (Ishikawa et al., 2014) in three important ways.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the current work relative to prior work.

claim: External feedback (food reward) was used as the reinforcer instead of intracranial stimulation.
source: First, we used external feedback (food reward) as the reinforcer instead of intracranial stimulation, a change which makes the paradigm more amenable to clinical translation.
evidence: This describes a methodological difference from prior work.

claim: The training was administered in the context of a spatial memory task.
source: Second, we administer the training in the context of a spatial memory task, which allows us to show that the neurofeedback training itself does not impose a cognitive burden.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The SWR events observed in the neurofeedback condition contain interpretable, behaviorally relevant spatial replay.
source: Finally, we show that the SWR events observed in the neurofeedback condition contain interpretable, behaviorally relevant spatial replay, suggesting that they are likely to contribute to normal replay function.
evidence: This is supported by the replay content analysis.

claim: The neurofeedback paradigm extends existing approaches by modulating the occurrence of discrete memory-related events in the hippocampus.
source: Our findings also extend existing neurofeedback approaches by modulating the occurrence of discrete memory-related events in the hippocampus, in contrast to longer-timescale modulation of continuous oscillations (Engelhard et al., 2013; Klink et al., 2021; Reiner et al., 2014; Wang and Hsieh, 2013).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the approach relative to prior neurofeedback studies.

claim: SWRs during the targeted interval contain robust and diverse replay that represents experiences relevant to the current state of the behavioral task.
source: First, we show that SWRs during the targeted interval contain robust and diverse replay that represents experiences relevant to the current state of the behavioral task, indicating that our method of SWR promotion recruits physiologically relevant ensembles during SWRs, does not overly prescribe which ensembles participate in SWRs, and allows replay content to evolve and adapt to changing task demands.
evidence: This is supported by the replay content analysis showing preserved behavioral biases.

claim: The method of SWR promotion recruits physiologically relevant ensembles during SWRs.
source: First, we show that SWRs during the targeted interval contain robust and diverse replay that represents experiences relevant to the current state of the behavioral task, indicating that our method of SWR promotion recruits physiologically relevant ensembles during SWRs, does not overly prescribe which ensembles participate in SWRs, and allows replay content to evolve and adapt to changing task demands.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of diverse, task-relevant replay content.

claim: The method does not overly prescribe which ensembles participate in SWRs.
source: First, we show that SWRs during the targeted interval contain robust and diverse replay that represents experiences relevant to the current state of the behavioral task, indicating that our method of SWR promotion recruits physiologically relevant ensembles during SWRs, does not overly prescribe which ensembles participate in SWRs, and allows replay content to evolve and adapt to changing task demands.
evidence: This is inferred from the diversity of replay content observed.

claim: The method allows replay content to evolve and adapt to changing task demands.
source: First, we show that SWRs during the targeted interval contain robust and diverse replay that represents experiences relevant to the current state of the behavioral task, indicating that our method of SWR promotion recruits physiologically relevant ensembles during SWRs, does not overly prescribe which ensembles participate in SWRs, and allows replay content to evolve and adapt to changing task demands.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that replay content reflects current task state.

claim: Subjects likely learn to engage an SWR-permissive state during the targeted interval in which brain-wide neural activity and neuromodulatory tone also enter a SWR-permissive realm.
source: Further, because subjects learn to modulate SWR rate, rather than simply generating a single suprathreshold event on command, it is likely that they learn to engage an SWR-permissive state during the targeted interval in which brain-wide neural activity and neuromodulatory tone also enter a SWR-permissive realm.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed increase in SWR rate.

claim: Manipulated events could recruit downstream brain regions in physiologically relevant ways.
source: This increases the likelihood that manipulated events could recruit downstream brain regions in physiologically relevant ways.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the implications of engaging an SWR-permissive state.

claim: Gaining experimental control over the SWR-permissive state offers opportunities to dissect extrahippocampal neural activity patterns and neuromodulatory influences on SWR generation.
source: Gaining experimental control over this SWR-permissive state offers compelling future opportunities to dissect extrahippocampal neural activity patterns and neuromodulatory influences on SWR generation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research possibilities.

claim: The overall number of SWRs produced was not different between the manipulation and control cohorts when the post-reward period was taken into consideration.
source: Despite the dramatic increase in SWR rate prior to reward delivery, we found that the overall number of SWRs produced was not different between the manipulation and control cohorts when the post-reward period was also taken into consideration.
evidence: This is supported by the SWR count data.

claim: The existence of compensatory, potentially homeostatic, regulation of SWRs could be critical for adaptive behavior.
source: One can imagine that the existence of compensatory, potentially homeostatic, regulation of SWRs could be critical for adaptive behavior: an excess of replay could lead to intrusive, rigid memory or loss of behavioral flexibility, while too little could lead to forgetting or memory interference.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the functional significance of SWR regulation.

claim: An excess of replay could lead to intrusive, rigid memory or loss of behavioral flexibility.
source: One can imagine that the existence of compensatory, potentially homeostatic, regulation of SWRs could be critical for adaptive behavior: an excess of replay could lead to intrusive, rigid memory or loss of behavioral flexibility, while too little could lead to forgetting or memory interference.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential consequences of dysregulated replay.

claim: Too little replay could lead to forgetting or memory interference.
source: One can imagine that the existence of compensatory, potentially homeostatic, regulation of SWRs could be critical for adaptive behavior: an excess of replay could lead to intrusive, rigid memory or loss of behavioral flexibility, while too little could lead to forgetting or memory interference.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential consequences of insufficient replay.

claim: Important synaptic scaling properties of SWRs have been demonstrated.
source: Such possibilities are supported by evidence for important synaptic scaling properties of SWRs (Norimoto et al., 2018) and a prior finding that electrical disruption of SWRs during sleep caused increased SWR occurrence over longer timescales (Girardeau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Electrical disruption of SWRs during sleep caused increased SWR occurrence over longer timescales.
source: Such possibilities are supported by evidence for important synaptic scaling properties of SWRs (Norimoto et al., 2018) and a prior finding that electrical disruption of SWRs during sleep caused increased SWR occurrence over longer timescales (Girardeau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: SWR regulation occurs during waking as well as during sleep.
source: Our results show that this regulation occurs during waking as well as during sleep, and further suggest that it occurs on short timescales, such as between pre- and post-reward periods at the center port in the current task.
evidence: This is supported by the observed compensatory changes during waking behavior.

claim: SWR regulation occurs on short timescales, such as between pre- and post-reward periods at the center port.
source: Our results show that this regulation occurs during waking as well as during sleep, and further suggest that it occurs on short timescales, such as between pre- and post-reward periods at the center port in the current task.
evidence: This is inferred from the compensatory changes observed within trials.

claim: Multiple systems could interact to regulate SWR occurrence.
source: Moreover, our findings identify evidence for multiple systems that could interact to regulate SWR occurrence: in addition to learning to modulate SWR rate directly, subjects also learned to use behavioral strategies, such as changing the amount of time spent at a port, that had the effect of normalizing SWR counts.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of both neural and behavioral changes.

claim: Subjects learned to use behavioral strategies, such as changing the amount of time spent at a port, that had the effect of normalizing SWR counts.
source: Moreover, our findings identify evidence for multiple systems that could interact to regulate SWR occurrence: in addition to learning to modulate SWR rate directly, subjects also learned to use behavioral strategies, such as changing the amount of time spent at a port, that had the effect of normalizing SWR counts.
evidence: This is supported by the dwell time and SWR count data.

claim: No improvement in behavioral performance was observed due to the neurofeedback manipulation.
source: We did not observe an improvement in behavioral performance due to the neurofeedback manipulation.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral performance data.

claim: The lack of behavioral improvement is consistent with prior results showing a decoupling between replay and trial-by-trial decisions in this task.
source: This is consistent with prior results showing a decoupling between replay and trial-by-trial decisions in this task (Gillespie et al., 2021) and others (Carey et al., 2019); we predict that longer timescale manipulations of SWR rate (such as moving to blocks of neurofeedback vs delay trials rather than randomly interleaving the two trial types) would affect memory consolidation and would show behavioral impacts.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Longer timescale manipulations of SWR rate would affect memory consolidation and would show behavioral impacts.
source: This is consistent with prior results showing a decoupling between replay and trial-by-trial decisions in this task (Gillespie et al., 2021) and others (Carey et al., 2019); we predict that longer timescale manipulations of SWR rate (such as moving to blocks of neurofeedback vs delay trials rather than randomly interleaving the two trial types) would affect memory consolidation and would show behavioral impacts.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the current findings and prior knowledge.

claim: Various homeostatic mechanisms act to maintain SWRs and the associated replay events at advantageous levels in young and healthy subjects.
source: This suggests that in our young and healthy subjects, various homeostatic mechanisms act to maintain SWRs and the associated replay events at advantageous levels, potentially limiting the extent to which we are able to shift SWR rates beyond normal levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed compensatory changes that normalize SWR counts.

claim: It is possible to use behavioral feedback to modulate the rates of SWRs and associated replay events during a specific time period.
source: At the same time, our study demonstrates that it is possible to use behavioral feedback to modulate the rates of SWRs and associated replay events during a specific time period.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by the experimental results.

claim: In subjects with compromised SWRs, even a moderate increase in SWRs or replay could move the system back towards healthy levels and potentially improve memory performance.
source: In subjects with compromised SWRs, such as rodent models of Alzheimer's disease, even a moderate increase in SWRs or replay could move the system back towards healthy levels and potentially improve memory performance.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: The neurofeedback paradigm depends on the occurrence of at least a low endogenous rate of SWR occurrence.
source: Since the neurofeedback paradigm depends on the occurrence of at least a low endogenous rate of SWR occurrence, it would be important to implement neurofeedback training as a relatively early interventional strategy prior to extensive neurodegeneration, and training may take longer in aged or impaired subjects.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of the neurofeedback approach.

claim: It would be important to implement neurofeedback training as a relatively early interventional strategy prior to extensive neurodegeneration.
source: Since the neurofeedback paradigm depends on the occurrence of at least a low endogenous rate of SWR occurrence, it would be important to implement neurofeedback training as a relatively early interventional strategy prior to extensive neurodegeneration, and training may take longer in aged or impaired subjects.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the requirements of the paradigm.

claim: Training may take longer in aged or impaired subjects.
source: Since the neurofeedback paradigm depends on the occurrence of at least a low endogenous rate of SWR occurrence, it would be important to implement neurofeedback training as a relatively early interventional strategy prior to extensive neurodegeneration, and training may take longer in aged or impaired subjects.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential challenges in different populations.

claim: Reduced SWR rates in disease models could be caused by a failure of homeostatic regulatory mechanisms.
source: Our results also raise the possibility that reduced SWR rates in disease models could be caused by a failure of homeostatic regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed homeostatic regulation in healthy animals.

claim: If reduced SWR rates are caused by a failure of homeostatic regulatory mechanisms, then a neurofeedback approach may even more effectively promote SWRs in the disease case.
source: If this is the case, then a neurofeedback approach may even more effectively promote SWRs in the disease case, because it will not have to overcome internal regulation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential advantages in disease models.

claim: The current findings serve as 'proof-of-concept' results that can inform and shape the implementation and optimization of SWR-focused neurofeedback interventions in disease models.
source: Our current findings therefore serve as useful 'proof-of-concept' results that can inform and shape the implementation and optimization of SWR-focused neurofeedback interventions in disease models.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance and implications of the work.

claim: When combined with minimally invasive techniques for detecting SWRs and replay in humans, this technique could be adapted to patient populations.
source: Importantly, when combined with minimally invasive techniques for detecting SWRs and replay in humans, such as MEG (Liu et al., 2019; Nour et al., 2021), this technique could be further adapted to patient populations to assess whether SWR-triggered neurofeedback in humans could lead to similar enhancement or restructuring of replay, and ultimately whether such an intervention could be therapeutic.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential clinical translation, supported by citations to relevant human studies.

claim: Data from four male Long-Evans rats comprise the neurofeedback cohort of animals included in this study.
source: Data from four male Long-Evans rats (Charles River RRID:RGD_2308852; aged 4–9 months; 450–550 g) comprise the neurofeedback cohort of animals included in this study.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: Data from a cohort of four additional male Long Evans rats who did not receive neurofeedback training are included in this study.
source: We also include data from a cohort of four additional male Long Evans rats used for a previous study who did not receive neurofeedback training (Gillespie et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the control cohort.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of California, San Francisco.
source: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of California, San Francisco (Protocol # AN191130).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.
